name: Jean Hasbrouck House

location.text: Historic Huguenot Street, New Paltz, New York

dates.note: FOUR DATES ARE ON THE RECORD AND NOT ONE IS EDITED TO AGREE WITH ANOTHER. The node says 1721. The Library titles the item 'Jean Hasbrouck House, Hugenot Street, New Paltz' with 'Building/structure dates: 1712 Initial Construction', and the data page's own cover title reads 'Jean Hasbrouck House(1712)'. The same cover then states the date of erection as '173 2' and gives its authority: '(IJarked stone in east wall.)' -- a datestone. The National Historic Landmark nomination read at NPGallery says 'Originally built in l69k by Jean Hasbrouck as a small' (OCR of 1694). A datestone, a Library catalogue date, a nomination date and a museum date; the house was built in phases, which is the likeliest reason there are four.

The Jean Hasbrouck House, The Huguenot Historical Society -- National Register of Historic Places Inventory - Nomination Form
refs.note: The nomination calls the house one of the 'impressive examples of Dutch Colonial stone architecture remaining in the United States' and argues the point this node's own exemplar note makes: 'Although "built by a native of Calais, France (Jean Hasbrouck), in an area settled by immigrants from Flanders and the Lower Rhine, and by Huguenots who stubbornly isolated themselves for decades from the Dutch Colonists who surrounded them, we must nevertheless view this outstanding house as a variant of the basic Dutch style.'

survey.prepared: Historic American Buildings Survey, District of New York City, No. 4 New York; the cover reads 'Yjakafield Worcester,District Officer, Washington Depot, Connecticut' (OCR). Its stated reference is Reynolds, Dutch Houses in the Hudson Valley Before 1776.

note: Tranche 2, the Dutch trunk in America. THE PLAN QUOTE CONTRADICTS BOTH NODES' PROSE AND IS THE MOST USEFUL THING ON THIS RECORD. `hudson-valley-dutch` describes standing 'in a single low room lit from two sides', and `dutch-colonial-american` treats the Georgian centre-passage front as a mid-eighteenth-century Anglicisation; the surveyor recorded this house -- dated by its own datestone to 1732, and the node's own earliest fully-Dutch exemplar -- as having a central hall with two rooms at each side. Recorded, not reconciled: the survey is a 1930s two-page form and the house has been re-read since.
